prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Inside, Psychics, That

outputs.L1:
Inside me dwelt a small donkey. I did not believe in magic, but the donkey was helplessly devoted to it—psychics, illusionists, arthritic old men who could predict the rainfall by the ache in their bones. That was the year I struggled to walk. I overthought each step and could never find the rhythm. The donkey taught me anew: "This foot. Yes, now that one. And swing your arms as though you're walking into trial to be exonerated of a crime you most certainly committed."

Then came the trouble sleeping, for I had to crank the generator in my chest far too often. Sensing my exhaustion, the donkey finally drew it out—gleaming and new, like a silver dollar—and cast it toward a flock of birds who were forced to fly a long way before finding safety. I understood then that I was a large and dangerous man, harboring a donkey within me, and yet I felt utterly powerless.

One day, during a final lesson on breathing, the donkey asked what kind of jeans I was wearing.

"The somber ones," I said.

"Poor kid."

"Will you be staying on for a third year, donkey?"

"No. I believe it's time for me to go. I think I shall wait for you beside the crumpled river."

"Yes, I imagine you have many important matters to attend to. But perhaps, one day, I'll come join you—for a drink, or maybe just a brief nap."
outputs.L2:
A tiny donkey resided within me. Magic held no sway over my beliefs, yet this donkey couldn't get enough of it—fortune-tellers, magicians, arthritic old-timers claiming they could foresee rain. During that particular year, walking became a struggle for me. I analyzed every step too carefully and lost the natural flow. The donkey stepped in to show me again. "This one first. Then the other. And pump your arms like you're headed to court to beat charges you're clearly guilty of."

After that came sleepless nights, since I constantly needed to wind the engine lodged in my chest. Noticing my exhaustion, the donkey eventually pulled it free—gleaming and fresh, like a silver coin—and flung it toward a group of birds forced into a lengthy flight before reaching safe ground. That's when it hit me: having this creature living inside me made me someone formidable, even menacing, though the realization left me feeling powerless instead.

During what turned out to be our last lesson together, this one focused on breathing, the donkey inquired about my choice of pants. "The gloomy kind," I answered.

"Poor thing," it said.

"Will you be sticking around for a third year, donkey?"

"No, I don't think so. I believe it's time for me to move on—to wait for you near that bent and weathered river."

"I understand you've got important business elsewhere, but perhaps someday I'll stop by for a drink, or maybe just to rest awhile."
outputs.L3:
# The Donkey Within

I have always known there is a donkey living inside me—a stubborn, patient creature who believes in everything I have trained myself to doubt. While I nod along politely at horoscopes and dismiss the psychic's knowing gaze as clever guesswork, the donkey inside me nods for entirely different reasons. He believes. He believes in the tarot's bent corners, in the way tea leaves settle into shapes like sentences, in the quiet authority of a palm reader tracing lines that were, apparently, always going to lead here. I am the skeptic wearing my skin; he is the faithful one wearing my bones.

There was a time—I don't like to speak of it much—when my legs forgot their purpose. Walking became a foreign language I had somehow lost fluency in overnight. I would stand at the edge of a room and not understand how to cross it, my feet arguing with the floor, my knees negotiating terms they no longer wished to honor. It was the donkey who taught me again. Patiently, without words, he showed me the rhythm—left, then right, then the shift of weight, then trust. He walked beside me in whatever place donkeys walk when they are inside a person, hoof-falls matching my hesitant steps, until walking became mine again, or maybe became his gift to me, on loan.

Later, there were nights that would not end—weeks where sleep refused to come because something in me, some engine, some generator humming beneath my ribs, worked too hard, burned too bright, refused to power down. I lay awake listening to my own machinery. And it was the donkey, again, who intervened. He did not ask permission. He simply reached in, past whatever barrier separates a man from his own inner workings, and pulled the generator out—wires and all, still sparking—and threw it as far from me as he could manage. I remember the birds. I remember how they scattered from every tree for a mile, startled into the sky, fleeing some disturbance they could feel but not see. The generator landed somewhere I will never find it, and finally, finally, I slept.

It was only afterward that the full weight of it settled on me: I contain a donkey capable of disassembling parts of myself I did not know were removable. A donkey who reaches into my architecture and edits it. There is something dangerous in this—in housing a creature with such casual power over my own machinery, my own legs, my own capacity for rest. And yet there is something futile in the danger too, because what could I possibly do about it? You cannot argue with a donkey who already knows, who has always known, who consults forces I have no access to and acts according to certainties I will never share. I am dangerous by proxy and powerless by design.

After years of this—years of his corrections, his interventions, his quiet mystic confidence—the donkey has told me he is leaving. Not abandoning, he clarifies, just going ahead. He says he will wait for me by a crumpled river, a river he describes as if it were a piece of paper someone balled up in frustration and then, out of guilt, tried to smooth back out, leaving all those creases where the water now has to bend and double back on itself.

I did not ask him why the river is crumpled. Some things, I have learned, do not survive translation into the language I use for the rest of my life.

I only told him that I might come find him there, someday. That when I am done with walking on my own, when the next generator inside me finally over-labors itself into silence, when I have no more use for the doubting man I've been—I may follow the sound of hooves to that bent water and see if he is still standing there, waiting, believing in whatever comes next the way he has always believed in everything I could not.
outputs.L4:
There were mornings when my legs forgot what they were for. I would stand at the edge of the bed, one hand pressed against the wall, and stare down at my own feet as if they belonged to someone else, some stranger who had wandered into my shoes overnight and left them there, heavy and unfamiliar. Walking became a negotiation. Each step required a small treaty between what my body used to know and what it now refused to remember.

It was around this time that the donkey appeared.

I do not mean this as metaphor, though I understand it must sound that way. The donkey was there in the grey hours before dawn, standing at the foot of my bed with an expression of patient, almost bureaucratic concern, as though it had been assigned to my case and intended to see it through properly. It did not speak so much as suggest—a kind of pressure behind the eyes, a nudging in the base of the skull that arranged itself into thought.

*You have forgotten how to walk,* the donkey said, without judgment. *We will have to start over.*

And so we did. The donkey showed me things I had once known and lost somewhere in the fog of exhaustion—how to shift weight from heel to toe, how to let the arms swing loose instead of clutching at the air for balance. Some nights it demonstrated by trotting in small circles at the foot of the bed, its hooves leaving no mark on the carpet, and I would watch and something in my hips would remember, distantly, the way water remembers the shape of a container it once filled.

Sleep was harder. The donkey had less patience for sleep, I think, because sleep could not be taught so much as coaxed, bribed, tricked into arriving. It would stand sentry by the window while I lay rigid and wide-eyed, and occasionally it would breathe out through its nose in a long, slow exhale that somehow synchronized with my own, until my ribs stopped fighting the air and let it simply come and go.

There was, at some point, a heart. I do not know how else to describe it—not the organ itself but something adjacent to it, a mechanism I had apparently been carrying all these years without realizing how much it weighed. The donkey found it first. It nosed at my chest one evening with unusual insistence, the way an animal noses at a wound it senses beneath fur and skin, and said, *This is not yours to keep. This is why you are so tired.*

I asked what it was.

*A ledger,* the donkey said. *All the debts you thought you owed. All the accounts you kept open long after they should have closed.*

We took it out together, though I could not tell you the mechanics of the procedure—only that it involved a great deal of quiet, and the donkey standing very still with its head bowed, as though performing something between surgery and prayer. Afterward I slept for eleven hours and woke without the particular grinding fatigue that had colored every one of my days for longer than I could remember.

Things became easier after that. Not easy—I want to be honest about this—but easier. I relearned how to hold a cup without my hand trembling toward spillage. I relearned how to climb stairs without counting each one like a small, private penance. The donkey grew quieter as these things returned to me, satisfied in the way that teachers are satisfied when a student finally stops needing them, though it never left entirely. It simply receded to the edges of rooms, watching, occasionally correcting.

Then, on an afternoon that gave no particular indication of its own significance, the donkey told me it would be leaving.

*Not far,* it said, when it saw my face. *I will be waiting for you. By the river.*

I asked which river, though I think I already understood there was no need to ask, that there was only one river that mattered, and that I would know it when I saw it.

*The crumpled one,* the donkey said, as if this clarified everything, and in a strange way it did. I pictured it immediately—not a river flowing smooth and silver through some pastoral scene, but one that had been folded and refolded like paper, creased with the marks of everything that had ever moved through or across it, its surface catching light in broken, uneven fragments rather than one long unbroken shine.

I understood, then, without being told outright, what the donkey meant, what waiting by that particular river signified. I thought I might feel afraid. I had spent so many months afraid of smaller things—of my own legs failing beneath me, of nights that stretched on without sleep, of the slow erosion of a body I had once trusted without thinking about it at all. But this fear did not come. Instead there was something quieter, something almost like relief, the way you feel relief upon finally setting down a bag you have carried so long you'd forgotten it was heavy.

*I'll see you there, then,* I said.

The donkey nodded, in its unhurried way, and turned to go, its outline growing thin and imprecise at the edges, the way morning fog thins when the sun finally commits to rising. I did not try to stop it. I only watched, and felt, for the first time in longer than I could say, something like peace settle into the space where all that old exhaustion used to live—patient, unafraid, already half turned toward the water.
outputs.L5:
# Inside Psychics That Claim to See Beyond

The world of psychics has fascinated and divided people for centuries. From storefront palm readers to television mediums with massive followings, those who claim psychic abilities occupy a curious space between entertainment, spirituality, and controversy.

## What Psychics Claim to Do

Self-identified psychics assert they can perceive information beyond ordinary human senses—predicting future events, communicating with the deceased, reading auras, or sensing emotions and thoughts that others cannot access. Methods vary widely: tarot cards, astrology, palm reading, crystal balls, or simply claimed intuitive impressions received during a session with a client.

Many practitioners describe their gift as something they've possessed since childhood, often framing it as inherited from a family member or awakened after a significant life event. Others attend courses or apprenticeships to develop what they consider latent sensitivities.

## The Business Behind the Practice

Modern psychic services have evolved far beyond the traditional storefront. Phone hotlines, mobile apps, and video consultations have transformed psychic reading into a global industry worth billions of dollars annually. Clients seek guidance on relationships, career decisions, health concerns, and grief processing.

This commercial dimension raises important questions. Reputable researchers and skeptics point out that techniques like "cold reading"—making educated guesses based on general statements and reading client reactions—can create convincing illusions of insight without any actual paranormal ability involved.

## The Scientific Perspective

Scientific investigation into psychic phenomena has been extensive, yet no controlled study has definitively proven the existence of psychic abilities. Organizations offering monetary prizes for demonstrable psychic powers under scientific conditions have never had a successful claimant. Psychologists suggest that the perceived accuracy of readings often stems from confirmation bias, the Barnum effect (where vague statements feel personally significant), and the natural human tendency to seek patterns and meaning.

## Why People Seek Psychics Anyway

Despite scientific skepticism, millions continue seeking psychic guidance. For many, these sessions serve therapeutic purposes—offering comfort during grief, a sense of control during uncertainty, or simply an outlet to discuss personal struggles with someone who listens without judgment. The experience itself, regardless of its metaphysical validity, can provide genuine emotional value.

## A Balanced View

Understanding what happens inside the world of psychic practice requires holding two truths simultaneously: the lack of scientific evidence for supernatural abilities, and the very real psychological and emotional needs that draw people to seek such services. Whether viewed as entertainment, fraud, or genuine spiritual practice, psychics remain a persistent fixture of human culture—reflecting our enduring desire to find meaning, connection, and answers to life's uncertainties.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal short prose poem about an inner animal companion who teaches the narrator how to walk, sleep, and breathe.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Animal Who Waited

Before I learned my own name, something four-legged and patient set up residence beneath my sternum, and has lived there since, teaching me the old ways I keep forgetting.

It teaches walking first: *lift the heavy foot like it's an apology, set it down like a question.* I stumble anyway. It circles back, unbothered, has all the time that exists inside a chest.

Sleep, it says, is not a door but a field you enter sideways. It shows me by curling smaller and smaller until it becomes a comma, a pause between one worry and the next. I mimic this badly for years before my body remembers it was always an animal too.

Breathing is the hardest lesson. *In,* it says, *like you're gathering something you dropped. Out, like you're finally putting it down.* I hold my breath for entire decades out of habit, out of some old forgetting, and it waits, ribs against my ribs, patient as a stone that used to be a mountain.

Some nights I feel it pacing, nose to the walls of me, checking the perimeter of everything I am. Other nights it sleeps so still I mistake it for my own bones settling.

It has no name I've found yet. When I ask, it just breathes—slow, correct, ancient—until I remember to do the same.

We are, the two of us, still learning to be one animal.
We are, the two of us, still walking each other home.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a piece of flash fiction in a dreamlike, absurdist style involving a talking donkey living inside a person's body.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Donkey in Mr. Feldman's Chest

Mr. Feldman first heard the donkey on a Tuesday, somewhere between his sternum and his second cup of coffee.

"You're breathing wrong," said the donkey.

Mr. Feldman set down his mug. "Excuse me?"

"All that shallow nonsense. You're a person, not a teacup." The voice had the particular patience of someone who had been complaining about this for years without anyone listening. "I've lived here eleven years and you've never once breathed properly."

He went to the doctor, who shone a light in his ears and told him to relax more.

"There's a donkey in my chest," Mr. Feldman said.

"There's a donkey in everyone's chest," the doctor said, not looking up from his clipboard. "Try yoga."

The donkey did not care for yoga. It brayed through the poses, unimpressed. "This is not natural," it said, as Mr. Feldman folded himself into a shape resembling a question mark. "In my day, we simply stood in fields."

"You don't have a day. You live in my ribcage."

"I have opinions about grass I cannot substantiate. That's a kind of day."

Weeks passed. The donkey developed preferences—it liked rain, hated elevators, wept (Mr. Feldman assumed it was weeping; there was a dampness, a heaviness in his lungs) during commercials for long-distance phone plans. It began narrating his life back to him in a voice thick with hay and something like tenderness.

"You are lonely," the donkey said one night, "in a way that has nothing to do with other people."

"That's absurd."

"I am a donkey in your chest. Absurd left the building years ago."

Mr. Feldman considered this. Outside, the rain the donkey loved was falling in gray ribbons, and something in his ribs unclenched, just slightly, like a fist opening.

"Stay," he said, though he wasn't sure if he meant it for the donkey or the rain or himself.

"Where would I go?" the donkey said, and shifted, warm and enormous, into the shape of his heart.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write something in the tone of a whimsical, melancholic fable—part magical realism, part therapy metaphor—about a man and the small donkey inside him.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Man Who Kept a Donkey

There was once a man who carried inside his chest a small grey donkey, and had carried it since he was seven years old.

The donkey was not large — no bigger than a loaf of bread — but it was stubborn in the particular way of small things that have been frightened once and never forgotten it. It planted its hooves when the man tried to speak in rooms full of strangers. It brayed, softly but insistently, at three in the morning, waking him with worries shaped like nothing in particular. When the man fell in love, the donkey sat down in the middle of his ribs and would not budge, and the man had to love around it, awkwardly, like furniture arranged around a pillar that shouldn't be there but is.

For many years the man was furious with the donkey. He tried to starve it, ignore it, drown it in rivers of work and wine. He would say to it, through gritted teeth, in the dark: *why are you still here, why won't you leave, I did not ask for you.* But the donkey only flattened its ears and waited, the way animals do when they know that weather passes.

It was not until the man was much older — grey himself, now, to match — that someone gently suggested he might try feeding it.

*Feed it what,* the man asked, bewildered, because you cannot exactly bring hay into your own sternum.

*Feed it attention,* the woman said. *Feed it the truth about why it's frightened. Most donkeys, when you get right down to it, only ever wanted a name and a bit of shade.*

So the man began to sit with the donkey in the evenings, in the quiet, and asked it what it remembered. And the donkey — who had been waiting fifty years to be asked — told him about a night long ago, a door slammed, a voice raised, a small boy who had learned that love could vanish like weather. The donkey had planted itself in the boy's chest that very night, thinking: *I will not let this ground move again. I will hold this place so still that nothing can ever be taken from it.*

The man wept, a little, hearing this. Not because it was new information, but because it was the first time anyone had thought to translate the bray into English.

He did not get rid of the donkey. You do not get rid of donkeys; this is well known among people who keep them. But he built, in the pasture of himself, a small shed with a slanted roof, and he began to visit it daily, and he stopped being surprised when, on the mornings of important things — weddings, interviews, doctors' appointments — the donkey planted its feet and would not move.

*I know,* he'd say to it now, instead of cursing. *I know. You're not trying to ruin this. You're trying to keep us both alive.*

And strangely, gently, on the days he said this, the donkey's ears would lift, just slightly, and after a moment — not always, but sometimes — it would agree to walk beside him anyway.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a strange, poetic short story with surreal imagery (a generator in the chest, a silver dollar tossed to birds, a crumpled river) exploring themes of self-doubt and inner guidance.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Generator

There is a generator in his chest, though no one told him when it was installed. It hums on bad nights, converting doubt into a low electric grief that lights nothing, warms nothing, only runs.

He walks to the river because the river is crumpled, folded wrong by some enormous hand, and he likes to watch the water try to iron itself flat again. It never quite manages. Neither does he.

*You are doing this wrong,* says the generator.

*You have always been doing this wrong.*

He takes the silver dollar from his pocket — his grandmother's, kept for no reason he can name — and he throws it to the birds gathered on the crumpled bank. The birds are not fooled. They know a coin is not bread. But they descend anyway, a black weather of wings, because sometimes the gesture is the point and not the gift.

The coin disappears into a fold of the river. Just like that: swallowed by the crease. He thinks, *that is where I keep my good ideas,* and does not know if this is true or only sounds true, which is its own kind of trouble.

The generator hums louder.

But underneath the hum, if he presses his ear to his own sternum the way you'd press an ear to a wall to hear the neighbors — underneath, there is something else. A smaller sound. Not electric. Something like a woman singing two rooms away, words indistinct, tune familiar as blood.

*This is not wrong,* the small sound says, or maybe doesn't say — maybe he invents it, the way he invented the meaning of the coin, the way the birds invented the coin's likeness to bread.

The river will not flatten tonight. The birds will not find the dollar. The generator will not stop.

But he stays at the water's crumpled edge anyway, one hand on his own chest like a man checking for a heartbeat he's not sure he's allowed to have, and he listens for the small sound under the hum, the singing under the static, the shape his grandmother's coin made in the air before the river closed over it —

that arc, silver, brief —

that was his, at least. That much was his.

He walks home in the dark, letting the generator run, letting the small song run under it, both true, both his, the crumpled river folding itself around whatever he leaves behind, the way doubt folds around a self and calls it *shape,* calls it *keeping.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental micro-fiction piece with quirky dialogue between a narrator and an imaginary creature that lives inside them, ending on a bittersweet note about parting ways.
counterfactuals.output:
**THE THING THAT LIVES BEHIND MY STERNUM**

*i.*

He introduces himself as Gully, though he admits this isn't his real name, just the sound he makes when he's nervous. He's about the size of a fig, mostly elbows, and he's been living behind my sternum since I was nine and broke my arm falling out of the Kowalskis' oak tree.

"You didn't cry," he says, by way of explanation. "So I moved in. Someone had to."

*ii.*

Some nights he wants to talk about weather patterns on planets that don't exist.

"Glorbon Six," he says, "has rain made entirely of forgotten passwords. You'd love it. Everyone's always logging back in."

"That's not a real place, Gully."

"Neither is disappointment, technically. Doesn't stop it from raining."

*iii.*

He has opinions about my ex.

"She had a laugh like a dropped fork," he says. "I mean that as a compliment. Forks are underrated. Very few things startle you awake *and* set the table."

I ask him what my laugh sounds like.

He goes quiet for the length of one whole traffic light. "Like someone finding a twenty in an old coat," he finally says. "Rare. Worth telling people about."

*iv.*

When my mother died he didn't say anything clever for three weeks. He just sat very still, a small warm coal, and once, around 3 a.m., he said, "I'm not going anywhere," which was the least funny thing he'd ever said and the only thing I needed.

*v.*

"Do you ever get tired," I ask, "of living in someone else's ribs?"

"It's not the ribs I mind," he says. "It's the echo. Everything you feel, I feel twice — once as you, once as the sound bouncing back."

"That sounds exhausting."

"It's the best apartment I've ever had," he says, and I can't tell if he's lying, and I decide it doesn't matter.

*vi.*

Lately there are gaps. I'll go a whole Tuesday without hearing him. I'll laugh at something and realize the sound didn't need translating first, didn't pass through his small furred hands before it reached my mouth.

"You're doing it without me," he says one evening, not unkindly. There's something in his voice like a man watching a bus he already knows he won't be catching.

"Doing what?"

"Being sad. On your own. Successfully."

I don't know what to say to that, so I say nothing, which turns out to be the correct answer.

*vii.*

The last conversation is short. He's smaller than I remember — not shrinking exactly, more like a photograph left in the sun, still there, just less insistent about its own colors.

"I used to think you needed a guide," he says. "Turns out you just needed company while you found the map yourself."

"Where will you go?"

"Where all good imaginary things go. Nowhere dramatic. Maybe I'll be a shape in a cloud someone's kid points at. Maybe I'll just be the reason you're gentle with strange, lonely things."

"I don't want you to go."

"I know," he says. "That's how you'll know it's time."

*viii.*

I keep expecting to feel the hollow where he was, the way your tongue keeps visiting a missing tooth. But it isn't hollow. It's more like a room after the movers have left — dust outlines on the floor where furniture used to sit, and all that light finally allowed to reach the corners.

Some nights, if I'm very quiet, I think I hear something like *Glorbon Six* drift up from underneath my ribs, faint as a radio station from three towns over.

I never answer.

I think that's the point.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
